interactions.title: Leaving home: flight, curiosity and a call to protect
lines: DM: [garbled] in the—so as you—back in game, as you drift, you begin to hear a rhythmic, pulsing noise and a vision of strange water-filled dream. There's water everywhere around you. And you think maybe you see faces forming in this current as you begin to drift down.

DM: They seem to be screaming. Somehow their mouths are open, but not speaking any language that anyone could ever understand, because it's not a language of sound or sight. It's a language of the saltiness of the water, the subtle gradients of temperature and pressure that that that signal the descent from the light zone to the darker areas of the ocean below, the pull of the currents, the movement of the water deep beneath the surface.
Seeker: Seeker's fascinated because it's like the motion, the bones of the mountain range, but sped up by a million 1 million times.
DM: Yes. And what these faces seem to be speaking of that seem to be dreaming about is desperate flight, ripped from somewhere, everywhere, nowhere. It's hard to know.

DM: Finding a door pulled open and the—not just—not just pulled open, but violently wrenched open, and in the process of being wrenched open, tearing holes everywhere in the world. And flowing, running, as the world collapses behind you. The searing heat of dryness. A concept that is seems completely alien in—in this language. Just nothingness, a void, and flowing down tendrils of magic from these gashes in the world. As everything collapses behind them, to a new place, a home of sorts, soothing, gentle, and alive.

DM: And the whispers seem to be speaking as they project these images of home and then violent, desperate flight. "We could not stay," they seem to say. "The home waters collapsed around us. The world waters were crushed. We fled, and we were lucky to find this place."

DM: And as they do, these faces seem to swirl around you, forming this long, thin, almost eel-like person, maybe you might call it, no mouth, but expressive eyes, who seems to think in your mind as they swirl through the currents, pausing, each of you in turn, saying, as the images of this act, of this flight from danger still play, and this echo, "We could not stay. We could not stay,"

DM: Says to Wellby, "Wellby, you could have stayed, stayed in the Green Sea with family and road homes and ship homes. Delwath could have stayed in tree homes and fey wanderings, could have not gone to war. Riswynn, could have stayed in deep mine homes and mountain homes and sheltered homes, and served your gods in quiet. Seeker could have stayed in ancient mountain homes and city homes and family homes. Yet you didn't," and it seems to be waiting. "Why?"

Wellby: Wellby says or thinks or imagines all those homes, the tidy, tight little ship cabins that he sailed in for years and years. The sound of the gulls over the water, the wagon homes, a little vibe, you know, cabins along with the wagons filled with trade goods. But also thinks and says, beyond all of those, this was my home.

Wellby: And remembers thinking back to all the different times with a map spread out on the table in front of him, all the different map shops and map sellers, and the little book of maps that his family had and the sea charts, and over and over again, putting a finger down across all different ages, from a little young halfling to grown man, on the blank places on the map and saying, "What's there? What's there?" over and over again, and at last says that it took me a long time to realize it down to my bones, but that's where my home really is. The blank places on the map.

DM: The ocean—The currents swirl around as Wellby's talking about that, and you can see images forming strange images: a massive island floating in the sea, giant city underwater carved in the side of a huge underwater mountain that stretches, for it's hard to say how far, because the water is murky and blurred in your vision, a ship—look—seen from below, nothing anywhere close to it, seemingly floating, and then somehow alive, diving below the ocean, its shape shifting as it does.

DM: And you can see you can hear the sort of just slight discordance in this, as the ocean seems to be acknowledging your—the strangeness of the world. And yet still there is this longing for what is now gone. But it swirls—the currents kind of swirl around Wellby, and as you, as you watch, as the rest of you watch, you see the—you know, the the the waters seem to sort of encircle him, and and he begins to drift a little bit lower, the rest of you sinking as the ocean waits for a moment to see if anybody else will speak.

Delwath: Delwath is thinking, and I guess speaking, but it's hard to express in words, of the dreaming, when he was a child of this place amongst the trees, where he would run and talk and play and explore and experience with his his age mates, his ka, his generation, all the things that humans experience in dreams that elves no longer do once they awaken from their childhood.

Delwath: And he recalls the stars shouting a warning from that place. Elmerca in particular, the elven Wild Star, shouting a warning into the dreaming: "War, awake! War, awake!" and waking up with his age mates, too young really to be awake to be taking up the burden of elven maturity, only 50, 60 years old.

Delwath: And the debate that spread across his age: "Do we—do we help or do we flee? Do we—do we march out of our fortresses and help the humans, help the dwarves, help the others, or do we stay protected?" And Delwath never doubted it was his place to march. Honestly, as he thinks about it, he doesn't really know now why something in that moment when he was awakened, that star shouting a warning. He just couldn't—and he never considered the idea that leaving home would be—that he would stay home, stay in the safety of his, the elven forests. From the moment he was awakened he he knew he would march.

Delwath: So it's, I guess, the—the—he almost feels the question is [garbled]—it's just not—he had to. There was no choice. And sometimes he wonders, you know, why did I do that. But it never felt like the raw—the right—it always felt like the right decision. Despite everything that happened. He's never regretted it.

DM: As the ocean circles around Delwath, you can see the—well, it's hard to translate into human emotions, because it's clearly not—entity, whatever it is, is clearly not human, but the pain, the regret. "We were not warned. We did not know what was coming."

DM: And it seems to—the water seems to cling heavily to Delwath for a moment, as Delwath also begins to sink. There's almost a sense of "we—" "We had no protectors. We had nobody watching over us, we had no divinity. We had to make our own power, and we were young then and weak. We would have liked a warning,"

before: Seeker: But we'll put Kong on the spot when he arrives.
DM: Yeah, I text, I'm texting him. I'm texting him as we go, so he'll at least, if he can manage to check his phone, be able to see a little bit of what's happening.
Seeker: Like depth measurements.
DM: Yeah, exactly.
Seeker: 43.
after: DM: As it begins to float away, sort of waiting for a moment to see if—waiting for a moment, as the rest of you begin to sink down. And and you see with that this seems to have triggered something. Da—the there's a shift in the in the ocean. And you hear the sort of melody, this low hum, begin and colors begin to grow in the ocean life: coral, fish, kelp, whales, starfish. And this talk of Delwath's story seems to have triggered something, and and "We had no protectors, but we became protectors."

DM: And you see this image of the ocean full of life, and this current, this water sort of flowing over the ocean. Hold on one sec. This current flowing over the ocean. The you know, the—sorry—the current flowing over life. Distracted, trying to get Kong to join,

DM: And as it flows across the fish you can see some of them swimming through this current and growing. Beginning to stretch, and their forms shift, growing legs, long legs with long toes with broad webbing between them, spread out, beginning to grow arms with long hands, with webbing spread out in this, and like, [garbled] fins that run down the sides of their arms, beginning to grow faces, eyes, mouth, stretching out the fish's face into sort of somewhat humanoid features. "We made something to protect," or it "made us to protect."
DM: And you can—
Delwath: Human—I mean, these look like merfolk. Are these—

interactions.title: Protecting a people, continuing the work and loyalty

Delwath: I just gonna ask one another quick—that at the beginning you were talking about this, like—I mean, the answer might be we have no idea, but at the beginning there was this impression of, like, what I took to be the the scattered planar weakness thing before. But maybe that was a misinterpretation. The the the whole thing that caused the scattered planar weaknesses that Rai was trying to solve, right? Or was it in pro—was the impression long, long, long—like, do we have—let me put it—if we do, we have any sense of time, or is it—
DM: Oh, yeah, this is all like, like—
Delwath: Everything they've been hinting at is from a deep past, not recent events.

DM: The the next image is—yeah. These these people, these fish men and fish women, as they stretch and begin to flex and open their eyes and look around. The current swirl around them, and they look to the currents. They look—the current looks to them, and there is something that passes between them. Understanding, a bond,

DM: And the ocean [garbled] and drifts, and as they do, the merfolk follow, staying deep, staying hidden, staying far below the surface. Dwelling in the water, dwelling in the deepness. And this sense, as you watch of time passing, people having lives, people building cities, learning to—or being shown how to weave kelp fronds into structures, how to coax the coral to grow, how to tame manta rays.

DM: And yet, at the same time, there's something very alien about this. There are no temples. There are no—you never see anybody worshiping a god. There are no—no writing. They seem to—they seem to be able to speak at great distance without speaking.

DM: And—and no, there's no—it's not the sense you get watching this. This isn't just the, you know, humans living underwater, right? There is something, like, deeply alien about this culture and something alien about this ocean that is swirling around you now, something—it's not—it's neither good nor evil. It's just strange.

DM: And yet the emotions that again triggered by Delwath's story that wash over you as you watch this are not strange, you know. It's the sense of you know, "We would—we too would go to war to protect this. We too see—know what you say when you are warned, and you must. And there's no choice but to fight."

DM: And as this image is growing, you see this sort of bitterness, or you feel—it's not—you can't see anything, but you feel it. It's like a bitter taste in the water, almost a metallic tang. And even when "We did not win. We did not give up. This was what we were protecting. This is why we stayed," and the ocean swirls around the—amongst this protectiveness and this motivation to to do whatever had to be done to keep these people safe.

DM: There was a question of—sort of probing at you. There were times. Why do—why did you keep going? Wellby, you were held by Grash's blade, and could have stayed in the memory of your people or turned to safer journeys. Yet you came back. Delwath, you found the answers to your questions, found a people who would celebrate you for saving their gods, and yet you didn't stop. Riswynn, you are twice renowned among the dwarves for recovering Chalice of the Runepriest among the Orcs for saving Xurkhaz among the most famous of all dwarves in the current age, and yet—and none could doubt that you had served the duty of your gods. And yet, and yet—and Seeker, you are offered a chance to join the ancient scholars of Tollen and learn the answers to every mystery of the universe, and would only cost 5 years of your life. And yet—and the question lingers.

Seeker: Okay. Why why not join the guild that seems to have all the answers? You know, I saw growing up, many leaving the fastness in search of fame, wealth, even just adventure. But I wasn't interested in that. I wanted answers. I wanted to understand how the world works, and for many years I thought that was the most important thing. And when I encountered that guild I thought they had all the answers. Now I'm not so sure.

Seeker: And I've also realized something very important about the people that I'm traveling with, which is that they just couldn't do it without me. I—you know, it's—it's not the magical explosions I create, or my ability to make them larger or smaller or magically help them with their tasks at at critical moments, or turn a demon into a worm; not my endless knowledge of the arcane either, without which we'd have no idea really what to do, mostly. I think it's—it's my ability to sit down on the beach and pick up what appears to be a random stone and notice some non obvious fact about the local geology, and in that way unlock the key to a puzzle. It's—it's—it's my curiosity that this group couldn't do what we do without, right?

Seeker: I think, at—at any rate, what use is that anyone else? It seems to be useful for this group of friendly people. And really I just want to keep finding those quests along the side of our journey to pursue. And so I I feel that this fellowship needs me, and I—and I need them in that way.

DM: The ocean kind of swirls around Seeker as he's talking. And—and you see—you see it, you see images that—that form kind of surrounding Seeker's memories and stories. And—and there's clearly something like, there's there's a part of this that the ocean or that that you're that this, this intelligence that you're interacting with doesn't quite understand. And and you realize, as you as you do like Seeker, so far is the first one who's talked about like himself, independent from the group, like being a part of a group like Seeker as an individual, and the group as a group. And this is not making sense to the ocean. You realize that it thought all 5 of you were one person.

DM: It seems to speak in the third person, talk about "we," but there is no sense of "I" yet. This isn't a bunch of different people together. And it's very—it sort of floats up to Seeker, curious as he's talking about traveling with a group and being useful to the group, and you—you get this sort of deep sense of, like, maybe puzzlement as it begins to whirl around Seeker, and you begin to sink deeper. Trying to understand what it might even mean to be to feel useful to a group of people who are not yourself, as it waits for somebody else to talk.

Riswynn: And when it asked Riswynn why—why wasn't she done with the fame and the achievements that she'd done thus far for her gods—she was thinking about how she sits around with her armor, and how back home he—she first realized the ways that she could be of service to the Bahrazel and her people through the mending skills that she had the that manifested first, as she became connected to the power she was channeling from her gods.

Riswynn: And she always tinkers with her armor whenever they whenever we're sitting around at a campsite, because you repair it, and then it breaks again. It's constantly in use, and that there's always a need for mending. And the history of the dwarven people and the peoples of Taelgar is long, and there are missing pieces that need to be found and reconnected. And she needed to find her people's shield, her people's cup. And she met other people who needed to be reconnected. You know the the giant with his eyes. And there are pieces that constantly need mending. The work of repair is never done. There's always a new—a new task, which—
Riswynn: Comes naturally to her reconnecting with the past.

DM: As—as Riswynn is talking about the—the need to—oh, there's always something that needs mending—there is this flash of an image of what looks like a city, or parts of a city, a great forest of kelp growing from the bottom of the ocean. But there's pieces of it that have rotted and are collapsed in amongst themselves, and it was a great gash that runs like a crevasse into the floor of the ocean that runs through the middle of this image, and you get this intense wave of failure,

DM: And the sense that it's not quite ready to—it doesn't—it's not—doesn't know you quite well enough to talk about what needs mending and where it—but you definitely get the sense, like, it resonates very strongly with this, and it feels—this intelligence, they, it—feels they failed, and there is damage in the world because of this. But it retreats. It's sort of the currents pull into their shell a little bit as Riswynn talks about this, and the ocean grows still for a moment as it kind of waits.

Delwath: Delwath says—starts by sort of saying, if the world had been different, I might have stayed there in the forest to the north, with the Ko'zula, if I had fallen from the sky in their forest and not met anybody else, perhaps that would have been where I stayed. The—but I didn't fall from the sky there. I didn't not meet anyone else.

Delwath: And he sort of talks about how his time away in the Shadow realm left him abandoned, disconnected from his elven family. He had given up on his elven age mates. He had given up on ever returning to the Elven lands like a normal elf.

Delwath: And he found companions amongst the humans and dwarves and halflings, and having found them and traveled with them and learned their strengths and their weaknesses, grown to care for them, for Kenzo's stories and tattoos and swift fists and Wellby's map making and excitement for new places and fondness for dangerous beasts with sharp razor claws and axe beaks. Yeah. And Seeker's obsessions and curiosity and dangerous lack of sense, and strong sense of self preservation, which go together, you know, and Riswynn's faith and ability to mend things and heal things, and that when he found the Ko'zula Delwath felt it was—it was too late. He had—he had found other people he was loyal to and could not abandon them, even though the forest to the north did feel like a place that could be a new home, and loyalty drew him back.
DM: You sense the current begin to kind of reach out slightly with this almost this hesitating kind of touch, this hesitating, creeping out, finding some—it's not clear of hope—hope, sorry.

Delwath: Okay, just add one. Just for the current too, I wanna add this sense of—Delwath will kind of explain the sense of the whole being more than the sum of its parts. Right? There is a thing that is the group of us that is not just the individuals of us. And part of that is also what drew Delwath back. It's the Comp—it's the Dunmari Fellowship with an emphasis on the word fellowship, that that is also something he is loyal to, just sort of, anyway.

DM: No, no, no, yeah, yeah. I get it. So it it hesitantly begins to creep out a little bit, and the current picks up slightly from where it had gone, very still with this this memory, and it—it—it—it's not—it's not clear whether hope is exactly the right word, or whether it's just a sense that maybe there is—see—something to grab onto, something to to look for.

DM: The the sense that what—what it seems to be latching onto as Delwath was talking is this sense that, but again you can—you can be loyal to something that's not yourself, and that this is something that probably maybe never would have occurred to it, because doesn't really think of other people. I mean, it doesn't really think of itself as—it doesn't think of individuals as individuals.

Learn to listen to it just, you know, very, very deep sense of humility, but to learn, but also like a—it's sort of like plugging into, like the the universal, like vastness, and like love of that of that ocean that the Stoneborn, the stoneborn, also possesses, but that Kenzo also, you know, feels like a very sincere connection to humility, but also an E—like an eagerness to serve, basically. Like, let me—you know, how can I? How can I also share about the wonder of the ocean to my people? So he—he kind of immerses himself in that deep in—in very sincere intention that he—without specifically being like, "Oh, yeah, I'm, like, setting up, like, a, you know, some monasteries. DM: And there's an image that the water below you clears, and you're looking as if through a mirror, but clearly not the present. Carefully coaxing these strange fruits to grow, bud off the kelp, letting them drift on the sea, to be eaten, and carry some strange essence of the memories of the people and the magic of the Sentient Ocean across the world—the Garden of Names.

interactions.title: The Ocean recounts Buruli, Gazankoa and the Garden of Names
lines: DM: So as you're all speaking the the ocean, the current goes still for a moment, and all is briefly quiet. And then you hear a humming noise begin, and in the currents, the whispers: "This is the story of Buruli and Gazankoa and the jade, and how we failed."

DM: And there's an image that the water below you clears, and you're looking as if through a mirror, but clearly not the present. This is a memory, and you can see this city that you saw briefly before, of a brief image of the kelp rot in the—the—you know, the the the city dead, now alive, bright and colorful, coral growing amongst the kelp, blooming, merfolk swimming and tending to it, [garbled]. Carefully coaxing these strange fruits to grow, bud off the kelp, letting them drift on the sea, to be eaten, and carry some strange essence of the memories of the people and the magic of the Sentient Ocean across the world—the Garden of Names.
DM: A memorial of a kind, but also a place of reliving, where the stories of all who had crossed through the ocean drifted in the currents and could be found again.

DM: And the power that—the—the way in which, as this green lights drifted through the ocean, the am—the power of this whispering garden just was that much stronger as the magic of this piece of jade illuminated the forests. But something changed coming of the jade. Now you see an image of—of a merfolk.

DM: A warrior, I'm—looks—there's almost a—a—yeah, forget that. He's—he looks—I mean, his face looks like I sort of described before. It looks almost like a fish. His eyes are sort of bulging a little bit, and he's bald, and it's got a fin running down the top of his head almost like fins where his ears are, stretching back, powerful, strong. But as you watch, you can see the way he looks at the garden with envy, with jealousy, not content.

DM: And then the whispers—can't see anything happening. Everything is inky and black. The mirror goes dark. But you hear this name, this word Gazankoa. And sacrifices and promises are made. And power springs to life in the heart of Buruli.

DM: And then the war, in the middle of the city, in the center of the great palace that once housed the names that was once the center of this garden, that where—the where the kelp grew into this twisting, spirally building of 50 feet tall, stretching halfway to the surface. Almost in the middle of that, a rift, creatures flooding out from the Plane of Water, creatures long—who have long held that the ocean is theirs to control, and this intruder must be—the intruder being the Sentient Ocean—must be corralled and controlled, threatening to spread across the deeps, until and then you see the ocean gathering its strength, and forming a bubble around Omi. Omi is the name of the merfolk City. And this deep sense of sadness as they watched the merfolk who are not part of this attack, who could not flee, trapped, enslaved, dragged back to the Plane of Water. But the contagion was stopped.

DM: Buruli fled through the portal again. Leaving only a small number to watch on this side. And now lives, dwells—the way is sealed. The the—the the portal is sealed by the ocean, but it can do no more. It cannot assault, cannot pass through, for if the elementals, the its enemies in the Plane of Water got a hold of even a fraction of its essence, they would get a hold of all of it, and so it stays. The rot cannot spread, but nor can it be healed until Buruli's power is taken from him and the magic of the jade that holds this portal open is brought back to this plane.

DM: And as you see this image, the story unfold in images and words below you, you can see the events, the fighting, little vignettes of what you think are memories of the ocean. Aha! The chaos at the beginning as many merfolk fled, and some were chased and hunted by Buruli's cult warriors, the desperate struggle to keep this crack, this rift that began to spread from growing and to contain it.

DM: As the violence of this vision of war and destruction and rot and corruption fades, and for a moment there's peace. And now you can begin to see the the water below you has become clear.
